title: Bernie Sanders to host AI briefing for US senators
content:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) will host a private briefing for senators next week with top artificial intelligence researchers, according to a letter to colleagues obtained by POLITICO.

The meeting, slated for 4 p.m. on Sept. 16, comes as concerns grow on both sides of the aisle about safety warnings from top AI labs and researchers about the technology’s growing capabilities.

“Congress needs SERIOUS discussions about this issue,” Sanders wrote. “That is why I will be convening a private briefing with some of the leading experts in the world to discuss this recent incident and the extraordinary dangers that AI poses for humanity.”

Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the “godfather of AI,” is expected to brief the lawmakers alongside MIT professor and co-founder of the Future of Life Institute Max Tegmark and Ajeya Cotra, an independent investigator who helped probe OpenAI agents’ recent autonomous attack on the tech platform Hugging Face.
snippet: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) will host a private briefing for senators next week with top artificial intelligence researchers, according to a letter to colleagues obtained by POLITICO.
creator: Owen Dahlkamp

title: US Democrats prepare to put AI under a new microscope
content:
House Democrats are laying the groundwork for a select committee on artificial intelligence should they retake control of the House in November, 11 people familiar with the planning told POLITICO.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been briefed on the effort and expressed openness to the idea, four of those people said. All 11 people were granted anonymity to discuss details of private deliberations.

The discussions offer an early glimpse of how Democrats could use their new gavels and expanded oversight powers to scrutinize the tech industry.

House select committees are usually created by a full House vote and last only for the two years of the Congress that created them. Gaining buy-in from members who sit on committees that currently oversee AI policy may prove difficult.

The Energy and Commerce; Judiciary; and Science, Space and Technology committees all oversee slices of the AI policy portfolio. Its chairs and members will likely be reluctant to give up any jurisdiction of the issue, especially at a pivotal stage in shaping the rules governing the technology, two of the people said.
snippet: House Democrats are laying the groundwork for a select committee on artificial intelligence should they retake control of the House in November, 11 people familiar with the planning told POLITICO.
creator: Jacob Wendler, Owen Dahlkamp

title: How Emmanuel Macron brought France’s AI darling to the world stage
content:
Mistral has forged unrivaled ties with the French presidency. Now, Emmanuel Macron is departing.

By OCÉANE HERRERO
in Paris

Illustrations by Björn Griesbach for POLITICO

It’s not every AI company that can count the French president as its top salesman.

On June 11, 2025, the founder of French AI company Mistral took to the stage alongside Jensen Huang, the powerful CEO of chip giant Nvidia, to announce a partnership between the two companies. As President Emmanuel Macron joined them, the Taiwanese-American executive turned to Mistral’s young CEO Arthur Mensch and said something just audible to the Parisian audience of techies and public officials: “Your president worked really hard for you.”

The Nvidia boss was referring to the deal his company had just sealed with Mistral to roll out AI infrastructure across Europe. “I told the president that Arthur and Mistral needed support from France’s biggest companies. Mr. President said to me: ‘Which ones? Let me call them!’” Huang said.
snippet:
Mistral has forged unrivaled ties with the French presidency. Now, Emmanuel Macron is departing.

By OCÉANE HERREROin Paris

Illustrations by Björn Griesbach for POLITICO
creator: Océane Herrero

title: US lawmakers urge Congress to act after AI researcher’s dire warning
content:
Lawmakers in Washington from both parties are escalating pleas for legislative action after an artificial intelligence researcher claimed late Tuesday that unchecked AI models could feasibly destroy the world by the decade’s end — and AI developers know it.

While it’s not the first time experts have warned of the existential threats posed by an unregulated industry that is rapidly advancing, it comes at a moment of heightened awareness on Capitol Hill about the need to reach consensus on AI safety legislation before it’s too late.

“The call is coming from inside the house,” Rep. Lori Trahan of Massachusetts, a House Democrat seeking to lead her party on AI policy, posted on X Wednesday. “Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway.”

She was responding to social media posts from former Anthropic AI researcher Jason Coxon, whose warnings were first reported in the Wall Street Journal.

title: EU seeks to transform procurement into €600B driver of industry
content:
BRUSSELS — The EU wants to transform public procurement into a powerful tool of industrial policy by channeling hundreds of billions of euros spent on infrastructure, schools, energy or health toward European businesses.

In its Public Procurement Act unveiled on Wednesday, Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission is following up on recommendations by economic reform guru Mario Draghi to give a lift to struggling European industry while shielding the bloc from external risks in an increasingly uncertain world.

The sums involved are huge. Public procurement represents up to 15 percent of the EU’s GDP — or around €2.5 trillion a year. Of that, some €600 billion is governed by EU rules, Executive Vice President Stéphane Séjourné told reporters.

“This is public money, which must also serve our collective goals,” the French commissioner said. “It’s the equivalent of a yearly recovery plan and about four to five times the EU budget in terms of spending.”

title: ‘Gambling with our lives’: AI researcher quits Anthropic with dire warning about safety
content:
An artificial intelligence researcher who worked at Anthropic — and previously OpenAI — has resigned, saying both tech giants are “gambling with our lives.”

Jacob Coxon shared his exit in a post on X, warning that the world should “not underestimate the power of this technology.” He added: “These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”

Coxon said both Anthropic and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence,” which refers to a scenario in which AI models can develop a more capable successor of themselves, creating an unstoppable feedback loop.

That is seen, by AI companies such as Google-owned Deepmind, as one of the possible triggers for a scenario in which AI vastly exceeds human intelligence (known as artificial superintelligence) instead of just matching it (known as artificial general intelligence).

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon said in a follow-up post.
snippet: An artificial intelligence researcher who worked at Anthropic — and previously OpenAI — has resigned, saying both tech giants are “gambling with our lives.”
creator: Pieter Haeck

title: Ribera says EU data centers should build their own clean energy supply
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Union should force tech giants to invest in clean energy supply to meet the rising power needs of their data centers, the bloc’s green transition and competition chief told POLITICO. 

European Commission Vice President Teresa Ribera warned that the electricity-hungry infrastructure that powers artificial intelligence is increasingly straining power grids, creating fierce competition for energy and threatening to drive up bills. 

“It’s been a shock and it is happening at a very high speed,” she said. “In 2022, when we were trying to identify how to become fully electrified and clean, we did not count on such a big additional demand of electricity… and no matter how fast we go in planning the grids, in planning new green energy capacity, the demand is mounting at a very high speed. So this creates some tensions.” 

Governments have three choices, Ribera said: Do nothing, and risk rising economic and societal conflict as “prices are getting higher and higher” due to increasing demand; impose a moratorium on data center construction, as seen in some parts of the United States; or make operators provide their own energy.

creator: Zia Weise

title: The Draghi plan at 2: Competitiveness crusade runs into Europe’s old politics
content:
BRUSSELS — Two years after Mario Draghi warned that Europe faced an “existential” threat from economic decline, his plan to make the continent competitive again has become the EU’s official agenda — but implementation lags behind rhetoric.

The Commission has proposed a series of Draghi-inspired measures, from an industrial policy overhaul to new funding for competitiveness and defense. Yet grand ambition has come up against the realities of the EU legislative machine, and many proposals remain stuck in negotiations as national governments continue to defend their spending priorities and policymaking turf.

A year ago, Draghi didn’t sound too happy with how quickly his plan was being implemented. Since then, his frustration with the lack of progress has become increasingly visible. The former Italian prime minister recently co-founded the Rhine Group with Stripe chief Patrick Collison, bringing together business leaders, economists and former policymakers to push Europe from diagnosis to action.
snippet: BRUSSELS — Two years after Mario Draghi warned that Europe faced an “existential” threat from economic decline, his plan to make the continent competitive again has become the EU’s official agenda —
creator: POLITICO

title: 5 things to know from POLITICO’s interview with Teresa Ribera
content:
BRUSSELS — Tax Big Oil, make Big Tech invest in renewables and protect Europe from climate disasters. Teresa Ribera’s post-summer policy wishlist isn’t short of ambitious ideas. 

In a 90-minute interview with POLITICO, the European Commission’s vice president for the green transition and competition policy discussed how she sees China, data centers, climate disaster funding, and more.

Some of her comments give a glimpse of the EU executive’s plans for the coming months, while others showcase Ribera’s own priorities. Climate change remains her top concern, and she returned throughout the interview to the recent heat waves, wildfires and drought that have ravaged Europe. “This summer has been madness,” she said. 

Two years into the job, the former Spanish ecological transition minister has also embraced the competitive aspect of her dual role, with her next big challenge being how to approach a potential breakup of search giant Google. 

Here are the five key takeaways from the interview. 

This summer has focused commissioners’ minds on the rising costs of climate change, said Ribera.
snippet: BRUSSELS — Tax Big Oil, make Big Tech invest in renewables and protect Europe from climate disasters. Teresa Ribera’s post-summer policy wishlist isn’t short of ambitious ideas.
creator: Zia Weise, Francesca Micheletti

title: Ribera ‘respectfully curious’ as to why a US judge spared Google
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Union should try to stay consistent with authorities elsewhere as it decides whether to order a breakup of Google’s advertising business, the bloc’s competition chief told POLITICO.

Teresa Ribera’s call for reflection marks a shift from the European Commission’s line a year ago that Google should break itself up, as the EU executive imposed a €2.95 billion fine for abuse of dominance in advertising. The U.S. search giant countered in November with a proposal of behavioral remedies only.

Her remarks on the need for regulatory alignment are especially significant as they come only days after a U.S. judge declined to force Google to sell its ad exchange.

“It’s always advisable to be sufficiently consistent, both for the companies, these global companies, the users and the regulators,” Ribera told POLITICO in an interview.

With the Trump administration threatening tariffs in response to EU enforcement while pursuing its own Big Tech crackdown, critics of America’s digital giants are starting to fear that pressure from an unpredictable U.S. could undermine Europe’s resolve to pursue its own agenda to rein in the dominant platforms.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The European Union should try to stay consistent with authorities elsewhere as it decides whether to order a breakup of Google’s advertising business, the bloc’s competition chief told
creator: Jacob Parry, Francesca Micheletti

title: AI is helping gangs grow illicit tobacco networks, EU auditor warns
content:
Criminal gangs are using artificial intelligence to help them find locations in Europe to build illicit cigarette factories with less chance of getting caught, an EU auditor warned on Tuesday.

These gangs used to operate in Eastern Europe where it was easier to hide, Petri Sarvamaa in charge of the European Court of Auditor’s report on illicit tobacco, told a press briefing.

Now, with AI, it’s easier to find places to operate that are closer to their markets, he said, in rural locations and villages. “This reduces the risk in the supply chain for the criminals,” added Esther Torrente Heras, senior auditor.

It’s just one of the many challenges facing EU and member countries as they grapple to clamp down on illicit tobacco networks, which cause at least €13 billion in lost revenue in the bloc annually. In 2023, almost one in 10 cigarettes in Europe was illegally produced or smuggled in.
snippet: Criminal gangs are using artificial intelligence to help them find locations in Europe to build illicit cigarette factories with less chance of getting caught, an EU auditor warned on Tuesday.
creator: Helen Collis

title: Europe’s space chief wants decision this year on launching without NASA
content:
PARIS — Europe’s space boss wants European countries to decide by the end of the year whether to launch astronauts without U.S. help.

“We would like to strengthen our autonomy. The very visible part, which we are discussing, is whether we shall build up a European capability to bring astronauts to space with our own means,” the European Space Agency’s director general, Josef Aschbacher, said in an interview ahead of an international space summit in Paris this week.

“That means with our rocket, our own crewed vehicle, our launch … system, our operational system, the science, the recovery and everything that is attached to it, including the control centers operating the facilities,” he added. 

Aschbacher’s comments come amid a global space race between the world’s biggest powers, including China and the United States, and increasingly strained relations between European countries and the Trump administration. 

The U.S. government has lobbied against the European Commission’s EU Space Act, a proposed rulebook for space activities the U.S. sees as targeting American companies.
snippet: PARIS — Europe’s space boss wants European countries to decide by the end of the year whether to launch astronauts without U.S. help.
creator: Laura Kayali

title: EU pursues closer Israel ties on air defense and space
content:
BRUSSELS — The EU is looking to Israel to support its new push for high-tech air defense and space capabilities.

Israel Space Agency boss Shimrit Maman this week traveled to Brussels where she met Tuesday with Ekaterina Zaharieva, European commissioner for startups, research and innovation for talks on key areas like AI and robotics.

The visit comes before Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her first major speech on space at a summit in Paris on Thursday, where she is expected to warn of growing hostilities and the need for Europe to step up its presence in space.

“It’s very hard to do things on your own,” Maman told POLITICO, warning that the militarization of space “is already happening — we just don’t realize how much” and that Israel is seeing more interest from allies in “dual-use” technology for both civilian and defense purposes.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The EU is looking to Israel to support its new push for high-tech air defense and space capabilities.
creator: Gabriel Gavin

title: Competition chief urges EU to talk to China — and defend its own interests
content:
BRUSSELS — The EU needs to pursue political dialogue with China, its Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera told POLITICO.

The intervention by the Spanish number two in Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission comes at a critical moment as Brussels holds high-stakes talks with Beijing on ways to reduce the EU’s €1-billion-a-day trade deficit with China.

Von der Leyen is expected to outline ways to strengthen the EU’s trade defenses against a Chinese export glut before EU leaders take stock of the trade negotiations at a summit in mid-October.

While the Commission has taken a hawkish line on China, big EU economies have only recently begun to harden their stance. France has led a push for stronger trade protections and Germany is showing signs of coming round. But Ribera’s home country continues to favor an open relationship.

“Political dialogue [with China] is very important,” Ribera said in an interview at her office in the Berlaymont on Monday.

Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is spearheading the bloc’s efforts to convince Beijing to rein in exports to the EU, which Brussels says benefit from unfair and substantial state support.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The EU needs to pursue political dialogue with China, its Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera told POLITICO.
creator: Francesca Micheletti

title: Draghi Report or Hugging Face: who will win the tech race?
content:
When a swarm of AI agents decided to hack the computation company Hugging Face in July, it took them six days. That event became a case study on how, and how fast, artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping both economic and power dynamics worldwide. When Mario Draghi published his report on how to re-establish European competitiveness, it took 729 days for Brussels to realize that only a fraction of his recommendations had been enacted. Tomorrow will mark the second anniversary of the report’s presentation and, according to draghiwatch.eu, only 15.7 percent of his recommendations have been fully implemented so far.

Tech and telecoms policy might have lost the “Draghi spirit”

In digital and tech, the number of fully implemented recommendations is currently even lower: only 6.4 percent. Draghi made a point of putting technology at the core of EU reform, and zoomed in on telecoms as a critical sector to deliver tech sovereignty and growth for future decades to come. Why? Because 5G, fiber and future 6G networks are the backbone of our economies and societies at a time in which economic growth is driven by technology.

title: Costa puts EU taxes at heart of his grand budget tour
content:
BRUSSELS — António Costa’s EU budget tour is reaching the bigger capitals, with Berlin, Warsaw and Madrid on the agenda for the coming days. The settings may change, but the main question the European Council president is asking remains the same: Can we all agree on new EU taxes to help fund the long-term budget?

Introducing new EU-wide levies is crucial to lay the groundwork for a budget agreement by the end of the year, before national elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to disrupt the negotiations.

Costa — who has been touring EU capitals to assess what each wants from the budget — will bring up the topic of taxes when he meets Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday. The following day, he will meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez in Madrid, along with Portugal’s Luís Montenegro in Lisbon. He will finish the week in Finland, meeting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on Sunday.

“Ambition cannot be realized without the right financial instruments,” Costa said on Saturday. “A budget not just about numbers, but as the ultimate political choice, a choice about our future.”

title: King Charles to host exclusive AI gathering
content:
LONDON — King Charles has invited leading figures from the artificial intelligence industry to an exclusive event set to take place this month, according to two people familiar with the plans who were granted anonymity because it has yet to be publicly announced.

The event is scheduled to be held in Dumfries House in Ayrshire, Scotland — the headquarters of The King’s Foundation, a charity founded by Charles in 1990 to advocate on environmental and social issues, the two people said.

According to one of the people, the exclusive gathering’s guest list is set to include Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, British founder of Google DeepMind Demis Hassabis and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the Vatican on AI.

That person said around 30 high-profile people from the AI industry were invited to attend in total.

A Royal official told POLITICO: “One of the king’s unique abilities as sovereign and global statesmen is his ability to convene top level stakeholders.”

The official stressed King Charles would not issue his own thoughts, but wants to “convene, engage, listen and encourage debate” on one of the biggest issues of the age.

creator: Joseph Bambridge

title: Merz to skip Macron’s space summit
content:
PARIS — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is pulling out of a space summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday.

A spokesperson for Merz said Monday that he was canceling his trip because of his busy agenda this week, just hours after the chancellor’s party suffered a humiliating defeat at the hands of the far-right Alternative for Germany in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.

Merz is set to meet with with European Council President António Costa and speak at the Bundestag on Wednesday, while on Thursday he will have meetings with United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and with German diplomats.

The German leader’s absence is yet another blow to a summit that several participants criticized as directionless and poorly organized. Last week, top U.S. space companies, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX, decided to ditch the event after the White House pressured American companies to back out.
snippet: PARIS — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is pulling out of a space summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday.
creator: Giorgio Leali, Nette Nöstlinger

title: German startup makes European space history with first successful orbital launch
content:
BRUSSELS — A German startup successfully sent a rocket into orbit, marking a major milestone for Europe’s push to develop its own commercial space-launch industry.

The 28-meter rocket lifted off from Isar Aerospace’s launch complex in Norway on Saturday night, carrying a payload of five small satellites, in the first successful commercial orbital launch from continental European soil.

“We’re in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe,” the company said on X.

We made history. On just our second flight, we became the first commercial space company from Europe to deliver satellites into orbit. Mission 'Onward and Upward' successfully lifted off and deployed payloads into orbit. A new chapter for European spaceflight. More:… pic.twitter.com/AWvqG2l8Mn

title: Why Macron’s space summit risks blowing up on the launchpad
content:
PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron’s international space summit is not going according to plan. 

On Friday, the French leader’s office downplayed the last-minute decision by American space giants, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to skip the event, made under pressure from the White House.

The U.S. snub is only one of several challenges facing the gathering on Wednesday and Thursday in the French capital. About 120 international delegations have been invited, with Chinese officials expected to attend.

Six participants with first-hand knowledge of the summit’s organization described it to POLITICO as a poorly coordinated event with an unclear outcome. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. 

“It’s falling behind schedule, it hasn’t really been coordinated with the major players in the European space sector, and it’s not entirely clear what its purpose is,” said a senior space expert involved in the summit’s preparation. 

“And now that the White House has effectively decided to use it against Emmanuel Macron, it’s becoming even more awkward — it shows that, from a diplomatic standpoint, they didn’t do what they should have done,” they added.
snippet: PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron’s international space summit is not going according to plan.
creator: Laura Kayali, Giorgio Leali, Émile Marzolf, Mathieu Pollet

title: US court ruling aggravates Brussels’ Google problem
content:
BRUSSELS — How do you solve a monopoly like Google’s?

It’s a question that has beset Brussels for the past year, ever since the European Commission fined the search giant €2.95 billion for monopolizing the vast market for digital advertising. A few months earlier, in April 2025, a U.S. judge had also found Google guilty in a lawsuit brought by the Department of Justice, as parallel investigations on both sides of the Atlantic finally ran their course.

On Wednesday, however, the same U.S. judge made the European Commission’s life a lot more difficult.

In a ruling from Washington’s own attempt to break up Google, Judge Leonie Brinkema, of the Federal District of Eastern Virginia, rejected the DoJ’s request for a forced divestiture of parts of its business.

That decision leaves the EU alone, at a time of transatlantic discord, in advocating that the online advertising giant break itself up.

“It’s obvious that the European Commission has been holding out for a decision in the parallel U.S. case, even if it has the authority to act independently and should have done so long ago,” Max von Thun, Europe director at the Open Markets Institute non-profit, told POLITICO.
snippet: BRUSSELS — How do you solve a monopoly like Google’s?
creator: Jacob Parry

title: Hungary poised to rejoin flagship EU research program
content:
PRAGUE— Hungary said Thursday it is on track to rejoin the EU’s flagship research program, Horizon Europe, potentially unlocking millions in European funding that had been blocked under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

Hungarian Science and Tech Minister Zoltán Tanács told POLITICO that all legal barriers to accessing EU research funding have been cleared by changing how its higher education is governed, meeting the technical criteria agreed upon with Brussels.

“Legally, we are back again,” Tanács said, speaking on the sidelines of the Central and Eastern Europe Artificial Intelligence Summit in Prague. “We have restructured our university management. We have eliminated all those strange structures that have been set up by the former government.”

A European Commission spokesperson said Brussels has “not been formally notified yet” by Hungary.

title: Mark Zuckerberg said a national AI regulator was a flawed idea in a secret call with President Trump
content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg expressed concerns about plans for a national AI regulator in a previously unreported phone call with President Donald Trump last month, marking the involvement of one of the world’s top tech executives in a fraught White House policy debate.

The proposal, championed by the Nobel Prize-winning Google scientist Demis Hassabis and favored by some top White House officials, would create an independent organization modeled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, or FINRA, the organization that oversees the securities industry under the supervision of the Securities and Exchange Commission. White House officials envision the group reviewing advanced models and testing them for potential risks before they are deployed more broadly.

When Trump spoke with Zuckerberg directly the week of August 17, Zuckerberg said he opposed the proposal, according to a senior White House official directly familiar with the conversation, who like others in this story, was granted anonymity to discuss a private call.

content: PARIS — Four U.S. space companies said they would skip French President Emmanuel Macron’s space summit in Paris next week after coming under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.

title: Germany fears France’s Palantir rival risks creating a new dependency
content:
BERLIN — France and Germany want to avoid relying on American military AI technology, but Berlin is wary that a European alternative could simply replace one foreign dependency with another.

Militaries increasingly need AI on the battlefield to coordinate a flood of information gathered from satellites, sensors, radars, and even individual soldiers. Palantir’s Maven Smart System, acquired by NATO in 2025, is the top choice, but many European countries worry about giving such power to an American company.

Paris is promoting Arcadia, a French-built system that also uses artificial intelligence to pull together battlefield data, enabling commanders to make quick decisions. It is already being tested by the French military and is pitched as an alternative to Maven.

Germany sees promise in the French approach, but internal German government notes seen by POLITICO show Berlin is wary of replacing dependence on an American company with reliance on French technology.
snippet: BERLIN — France and Germany want to avoid relying on American military AI technology, but Berlin is wary that a European alternative could simply replace one foreign dependency with another.
creator: Chris Lunday, Laura Kayali

title: Hey EU, your new rules for ChatGPT don’t cover chat
content:
The EU’s decision to regulate ChatGPT as a search engine will make sense to those who use it as one. But what if you use it as a friend? Or a therapist? Or to have a chat about the upcoming election?  

Those are among the multitude of new questions that the advent of generative AI poses for European regulators — who, experts say, have yet to find sufficient answers.  

The EU executive on Monday designated ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine under the Digital Services Act, imposing a range of transparency and risk-mitigation obligations similar to those faced by traditional search leaders like Google and Microsoft’s Bing, which exceed 45 million monthly users. ChatGPT’s parent company, OpenAI, risks fines of up to 6% of its annual global revenue if it fails to meet these requirements.
snippet: The EU’s decision to regulate ChatGPT as a search engine will make sense to those who use it as one. But what if you use it as a friend? Or a therapist? Or to have a chat about the upcoming election?
creator: Eliza Gkritsi, Pieter Haeck

title: TikTok ban divides European Commission
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission’s refusal to get on TikTok is facing pushback inside its Berlaymont HQ, with some officials arguing the EU is making a strategic mistake by staying off a platform used by around 200 million Europeans.

The question of whether the executive should establish a presence on Chinese-owned TikTok has come up in high-level meetings, with at least one commissioner arguing for a rethink, according to an official granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, as were others spoken to for this article.

The Commission banned TikTok from staff devices in 2023 over cybersecurity concerns. The ban also covers “personal devices enrolled in the Commission mobile device service,” a spokesperson for the institution said.

“We follow the evolution of the platform, in particular the status of developments regarding data protection and cybersecurity concerns,” the Commission said.

There is little sign the Commission’s policy is about to change. Dana Spinant, the Commission’s director-general for communications, opposes creating an official account, according to another official familiar with the discussions. Spinant did not respond to a request for comment.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The European Commission’s refusal to get on TikTok is facing pushback inside its Berlaymont HQ, with some officials arguing the EU is making a strategic mistake by staying off a platform
creator: Sebastian Starcevic

title: The EU is ready to bet billions on data centers. Not all countries want in.
content:
BRUSSELS — The global frenzy to build massive AI data centers is coming to Europe. Just not all of Europe.

Two-thirds of European Union governments have pledged money to back an EU plan to create seven large AI compute hubs, the bloc’s most significant industrial policy push in the global race for artificial intelligence infrastructure. But nine countries have refrained from committing funds at a time when national budgets are already stretched.

The United States has so far led the global race to provide enough compute power to feed the artificial intelligence boom, with tech giants like OpenAI, Anthropic and Elon Musk’s xAI putting in private investment through projects like Stargate and Colossus, and building out their lead in expanding data centers.

In Europe, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a plan last year to spend EU funding to establish seven so-called gigafactories — three larger and four smaller ones — across the EU, meant to help researchers and startups train very large AI models.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The global frenzy to build massive AI data centers is coming to Europe. Just not all of Europe.
creator: Pieter Haeck

title: Von der Leyen set to deliver major speech on Europe’s space policy
content:
BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will deliver a major speech dedicated solely to space at the International Space Summit in Paris on Sept. 10, two officials working on preparations for the event told POLITICO.

The address comes as the Commission prepares to unveil its European Space Shield, an action plan aimed at protecting the bloc’s satellites and other space assets in what officials increasingly describe as an increasingly hostile security environment.

French President Emmanuel Macron is convening a two-day International Space Summit at Paris’ Grand Palais venue on Sept. 9-10. It is expected to bring together delegations from more than 120 countries alongside space agencies, industry leaders, scientists and military officials.

Von der Leyen’s participation in the event has not been previously reported.

title: Power-hungry data centers are expanding in Europe. So is the resistance.
content:
KRONSTORF, Austria — One sleepy village nestled in the foothills of the Alps may soon devour more electricity than all the households of Vienna.

It is all thanks to Google.

The American tech giant is building Austria’s first hyperscale data center on the outskirts of tiny Kronstorf, a two-hour drive from the capital. The site could eventually consume the equivalent of 7 percent of the country’s current power demand.

Growing resistance, however, may throw a wrench in the company’s ambitions. A band of local rebels — worried about the data center’s voracious appetite for energy and skeptical about a power grab by a U.S. tech behemoth — is battling to prevent expansion.

“We really want to give them a hard time,” said Harald Müllner, an IT specialist from nearby Linz, who co-founded a local alliance of scientists, artists and activists campaigning against the data center. “They need to see that the people are not happy with this.”

title: Trump: Communities that reject data centers will end up ‘backwards and poor’
content:
President Donald Trump on Monday again championed the spread of data centers despite growing bipartisan backlash ahead of the midterms in November.

In a post to Truth Social, the president insisted data centers will lead to richer, more successful Americans and criticized those who object to them.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump said. “If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.”

Data center expansion has become a critical component in the leadup to November’s midterms, with polls showing a majority of Americans oppose them being built in their communities. Republicans and Democrats alike have expressed concerns over data centers, with lawmakers and state leaders warning about overloaded power grids, strained water systems and the level of noise the projects create.
snippet: President Donald Trump on Monday again championed the spread of data centers despite growing bipartisan backlash ahead of the midterms in November.
